title: N-Ch-M

segments.voice: Yesterday, G-A-L: the go'el, the near relative who walks to the gate and buys back what was lost. Your line was redeem. What did you take one step to buy back? Today, what family does when the loss can't be bought back. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

A house with the mirrors covered. The front door is left unlocked so nobody has to ring. Inside, the mourners sit on low stools, and visitors come in quietly with trays of food and sit down near them. By an old custom, the visitors don't start talking. They wait, sometimes a long while, until the mourner speaks first. And when they get up to leave, they say a set line in Hebrew, something like: may God, called here the Place, comfort you among the mourners of Zion and Jerusalem. The verb in that line, yenachem, comes from today's root.
screen: `A SHIVA HOUSE.` → `THE VISITORS WAIT.` → `MAY THE PLACE COMFORT YOU.`

segments.voice: N-Ch-M. Nun, chet, mem. Nechamah, comfort. Turn it four ways. First, the prophet. Isaiah chapter forty opens, in the King James: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." In Hebrew, nachamu, nachamu: the word said twice, as if once weren't enough. That chapter is read on the Shabbat after Tisha b'Av, the day of mourning for the Temples, and the Shabbat takes its name from the first word: Shabbat Nachamu. Second, a baby's name. When Noah is born, his father Lamech names him and explains it: "This same shall comfort us concerning our work and toil of our hands." The text ties the boy's name to comfort, after the curse on the ground that made work so hard. Third, Joseph. After their father Jacob dies, his brothers are afraid he'll finally pay them back for selling him. Instead, the King James says, "he comforted them, and spake kindly unto them." The Hebrew there reads, more literally, that he spoke to their heart. That's what comfort looks like in the story: not a speech about what went wrong, but words aimed at the heart. Fourth, back to the shiva house. Yenachem, may God comfort you. The visitors don't claim to do the comforting themselves. They sit, they wait, they bring food, and they hand the comfort back to the Place. The root holds all of it: a prophet's doubled cry, a baby's name, a brother's kind words, a quiet visit.
screen: `NACHAMU: COMFORT YE, COMFORT YE.` · `NOAH: THIS SAME SHALL COMFORT US.` · `JOSEPH SPOKE TO THEIR HEART.` · `YENACHEM: MAY THE PLACE COMFORT YOU.` · then, large: `נַחֲמוּ נַחֲמוּ`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person carrying something heavy right now. A loss, an illness, a job gone, a quiet loneliness. Picture yourself sitting near them, the way visitors sit at a shiva: not fixing, not explaining, just there. Now think of one short message you could send them today, a few words aimed at the heart, the way Joseph spoke to his brothers. Hold it until it feels right. If you pray, you can ask that they be comforted. The bell holds the time.
N-Ch-M. Nun, chet, mem: nechamah, comfort, from nachamu to yenachem. This week's roots ran soul, earth, keep, work, king, redeem, and comfort. Today's word.
Your line: comfort. Today, send that one message, short and kind, and don't add advice. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Visitors to a shiva house sit with the mourners, wait for them to speak first, and on leaving say ha-Makom yenachem, may the Place comfort you; the Shabbat after Tisha b'Av is called Shabbat Nachamu, after the opening of Isaiah 40, its prophetic reading.

notes: Quotations from the KJV; JPS 1917 Isaiah 40:1 reads 'Comfort ye, comfort ye My people, saith your God.' Confirm the Judaism path accepts KJV.
Moed Katan 28b: comforters may not speak until the mourner opens; paraphrased as 'an old custom' and 'the Talmud teaches'. Confirm.

The shiva phrase (ha-Makom yenachem etchem b'toch she'ar avelei Tziyon v'Yerushalayim) paraphrased; 'many say' describes a common custom, not a statistic. Covered mirrors and unlocked doors are customs, not universal; soften if needed.
Genesis 50:21 'spake kindly unto them' is vaydaber al libam, literally 'spoke to/upon their heart'; confirm.
Genesis 5:29 ties Noah's name to comfort (yenachamenu); the script says only that the text ties them.
Tisha b'Av described as 'the day of mourning for the Temples'; Shabbat Nachamu's haftarah is Isaiah 40:1–26.
